home.titleC: build all the way to GPT.
home.lead: Each level asks you to wire existing parts into a new one, which then joins your library. Sigmoid and softmax first, then backpropagation, optimizers and attention, and finally a GPT you train in the browser and that writes text.
chapter.0.desc: add, mul, exp, log → sigmoid, tanh
chapter.1.desc: Build derivative circuits, then let them calculate how to adjust parameters.
chapter.3.desc: A neural network is a learnable function: input → linear layer → activation → prediction; loss trains shared parameters.
chapter.4.desc: Number characters, turn them into vectors, then predict the next character. Training changes parameters; generation only uses them.
chapter.5.desc: Let positions find and mix relevant content, then use it to predict the next character.
chapter.6.desc: Stack information exchange and per-position processing into a GPT-style character predictor: train against known answers, then generate one character at a time.

levels.0-1.title: Negate
levels.0-1.description: Your first part: take x, output −x. All you have is constants, add, multiply, exp and log.
levels.0-2.title: Subtract
levels.0-2.description: Take a and b, output a − b. The Negate part you just built is now in your parts list.
levels.0-3.title: Reciprocal
levels.0-3.description: Take a positive x, output 1/x. No division, no powers. Tests use positive numbers only.
levels.0-4.title: Divide
levels.0-4.description: Take a and a positive b, output a ÷ b. a can be negative, so you cannot take its log.
levels.0-5.title: Sigmoid
levels.0-5.description: Sigmoid maps real numbers between 0 and 1: σ(x) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ˣ). An activation function goes after a linear calculation to add curvature; chapter 3 shows why a curved decision boundary needs it.
levels.0-6.title: Hyperbolic tangent
levels.0-6.description: tanh(x) = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ) / (eˣ + e⁻ˣ) maps real numbers into (−1, 1).
levels.0-7.title: ReLU
levels.0-7.description: New primitive: max(a, b) outputs the larger of the two. Use it to build ReLU: pass x through when it is positive, otherwise output 0.
levels.0-8.title: Square root
levels.1-1.title: Derivative of a square
levels.1-1.description: In this chapter you build not f(x) but its derivative f′(x), the slope of the curve at x. Start with f(x) = x².
levels.1-2.title: Product rule
levels.1-2.description: f(x) = x · eˣ. For a product of two functions: (u·v)′ = u′·v + u·v′.
levels.1-3.title: Chain rule
levels.1-3.description: f(x) = e³ˣ. For a composition, multiply the outer derivative (at the inner value) by the inner derivative.
levels.1-4.title: Derivative of log
levels.1-5.title: Derivative of sigmoid
levels.1-5.description: f(x) = σ(x). The derivative of sigmoid can be written using sigmoid alone, one reason it works well in neural networks. Pass and the derivative you build becomes the part σ′ for later levels.
levels.1-6.title: Derivative of tanh
levels.1-6.description: f(x) = tanh(x). Like sigmoid, its derivative can be written using tanh alone. Pass to get the part tanh′.
levels.1-7.title: Log chain rule
levels.1-7.description: f(x) = log(1 + x²). Combine the chain rule with what you have built so far. Next, functions will have more than one variable.
levels.features.autodiff: Autodiff unlocked: the "∂ Gradient graph" button above the canvas shows how the engine differentiates
levels.features.expression: Expression box unlocked: type a formula to generate its parts
errors.matmul_shape: Matrix multiply shapes do not fit: a is {a}, b is {b}. The last axis of a must equal the second-to-last axis of b.
levels.xor.hint1: One linear layer cannot separate XOR. Multiply x [4×2] by a parameter [2×k], add a bias [k], apply an activation, multiply by [k×2], add a bias [2], then softmax.
levels.xor.hint2: Set a parameter's shape in the Properties panel on the right. A smaller hidden size k means fewer parameters and a better score.
levels.0-1.hint1: What number flips the sign of x when you multiply by it?
levels.0-1.hint2: After dropping in a constant, set its value under Properties on the right.
levels.0-2.hint1: Subtracting a number is the same as adding its…?
levels.0-2.hint2: Only b needs to go through Negate.
levels.0-3.hint1: log turns multiplication and division into addition and subtraction. How does log(1/x) relate to log(x)?
levels.0-3.hint2: exp and log undo each other: exp(log(y)) = y.
levels.0-4.hint1: Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its…?
levels.0-4.hint2: Only b needs reshaping; a passes straight through.
levels.0-5.hint1: Start from the innermost −x and work outwards.
levels.0-5.hint2: You have already built Negate and Reciprocal. Use them.
levels.0-6.hint1: Multiply top and bottom by eˣ and only one exponential, e²ˣ, is left.
levels.0-6.hint2: One output can feed several wires: compute e²ˣ once.
levels.0-7.hint1: What should x be compared with?
levels.0-7.hint2: One max and one constant are enough.
levels.0-8.hint1: √x is x to the power ½.
levels.0-8.hint2: Remember Reciprocal: log turns powers into multiplication.
levels.1-1.hint2: The answer needs a single multiply.
levels.1-2.hint1: The derivative of x is 1; the derivative of eˣ is eˣ again.
levels.1-2.hint2: Both terms contain eˣ. Factor it out to save a part.
levels.1-3.hint1: The outer function is eᵘ, whose derivative is eᵘ; the inner one is u = 3x.
levels.1-4.hint1: log undoes exp: if y = log(x) then x = eʸ. Differentiate both sides with respect to x.
levels.1-4.hint2: The answer is a part you have already built.
levels.1-5.hint1: Write σ(x) as (1 + e⁻ˣ)⁻¹, apply the chain rule, then rewrite the result in terms of σ(x).
levels.1-5.hint2: σ′(x) = σ(x)·(1 − σ(x)). Compute σ(x) once.
levels.1-6.hint1: Use the quotient rule (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²; the numerator becomes (eˣ+e⁻ˣ)² − (eˣ−e⁻ˣ)².
levels.1-7.hint1: The outer log(u) has derivative 1/u; the inner part is u = 1 + x².

levels.shape_variant: Breaks when the inputs are {shapes}. Don't hard-code the shape.
levels.axes.title: Shapes and axes
levels.axes.description:
From this chapter on, a wire can carry not just one number but a whole block of numbers laid out in order: a tensor. Its shape lists how long it is in each direction: one number has shape []; a list of 6 numbers is [6]; 2 rows of 3 is [2,3]. The same 6 numbers can be laid out as [6] or as [2,3].
Each direction is an axis, counted from 0: in [2,3], axis 0 has length 2 (down the rows) and axis 1 has length 3 (across the columns). −1 means the last axis and −2 the second to last: however many axes a tensor has, −1 is the last one.
A node’s shape is shown beside its title; hover a node to see all its values.

This level: add up each row of x [2,3] to output y [2].
levels.axes.hint1: Summing along an axis removes that axis: [2,3] summed along axis 0 gives [3] (one total per column); along axis −1 it gives [2] (one per row).
levels.axes.hint2: Set Sum’s axis to −1. With “Keep dimensions” on, the summed axis stays as length 1 and you get [2,1]; turn it off here.
levels.2-2.title: Broadcasting
levels.2-2.description: Inputs x [4×3], s [4×1], b [3]. Output x·s + b. Different shapes still combine: line the shapes up from the last axis, and any axis of length 1, or missing, is copied until it matches the other side. This is broadcasting. Each number in s fills its row; the row b is copied onto every row. After that it is still entry-by-entry multiply and add.
levels.2-2.hint1: No new part needed. Broadcasting is built into add and multiply.
levels.2-2.hint2: Multiply x by s, then add b.
levels.2-6.title: Transpose, then multiply
levels.2-6.description: Inputs a [4×3] and b [5×3]. Output a·bᵀ [4×5]: each cell is the dot product of a row of a with a row of b. b has the wrong shape, so transpose it first. Transpose swaps two axes, by default the last two, so a batch axis in front still works.
levels.2-6.hint1: Turn b into [3×5], then use the matrix multiplication you built.
levels.2-6.hint2: Transpose with the default axes [−2, −1], wire it into matmul's b port, and a into the a port.
levels.2-1.title: Dot product
levels.2-1.description: Add and multiply work on tensors as before, position by position: multiplying two lists multiplies matching entries. a and b are vectors of length 6. Output their dot product: multiply matching entries, then add everything up. The judge also tries shorter vectors.
levels.2-1.hint1: Wire a and b straight into a multiply. You still get a list of 6.
levels.2-1.hint2: Sum along axis −1 with “Keep dimensions” off: the vector’s only axis is summed away, leaving a single number of shape [].
levels.2-3.title: Mean
levels.2-3.description: x is a 4×6 table. Output the mean of each row, shape [4×1]. The judge also feeds 3×5 and 2×3×4 inputs, so "divide by 6" won't do. The circuit has to count the row itself. Passing this unlocks Size: from then on you can read an axis length directly instead of counting.
levels.2-3.hint1: Sum adds up a row. What if every number in the row were 1?
levels.2-3.hint2: x × 0 + 1 is a tensor of ones shaped like x. Sum both (keeping dimensions) and divide.
levels.2-4.title: Outer product
levels.2-4.description: a has length 4 and b has length 3. Output a 4×3 table whose row i, column j is a[i]·b[j]. This is not matrix multiplication; it is the broadcasting from the last level. Stand a up as a [4×1] column, lay b down as a [1×3] row, let each copy out to [4×3], then multiply cell by cell. (Textbooks write a·bᵀ, treating vectors as n×1 matrices. These vectors are one-dimensional, so first add an axis.)
levels.2-4.hint1: Insert dimension adds a length-1 axis where you choose. Stand a up as a column and lay b down as a row.
levels.2-4.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for a and axis 0 for b, then multiply.
levels.2-5.title: Matrix multiplication
levels.2-5.description: Multiply a [4×3] by b [3×5] to get [4×5]. Each cell is the dot product of a row of a with a column of b. Matrix multiplication is not a new operation: lay out every product at once, the way you did the outer product (broadcast, then multiply), then sum away the extra axis. There may be a batch dimension in front, and then axis 0 is no longer the rows. So count axes from the end: −1 is the last axis, −2 the one before, however many axes come first.
levels.2-5.hint1: Aim for a [4×3×5] block of products: a becomes [4×3×1] and b becomes [1×3×5].
levels.2-5.hint2: Insert at axis −1 for a and axis −3 for b. Multiply, then sum over axis −2 without keeping it.
levels.2-7.title: Softmax
levels.2-7.description: Turn each row of x into probabilities. Take eˣ so every entry is positive, then divide by the row total. One test row sits around 100, and e¹⁰⁰ overflows.
levels.2-7.hint1: Subtracting the same constant from a whole row doesn't change softmax. Which constant is safest?
levels.2-7.hint2: Subtract the row maximum (keeping dimensions), take exp, then divide by the row sum of the exps.
levels.2-8.title: Layer norm
levels.2-8.description: Center each row at 0 and control its scale: subtract the mean, then divide by √(variance + ε), with ε = 0.00001. Unless variance is tiny, the result has variance near 1; constant rows become zero. This is not converting values to probabilities: it helps stabilize training when layers are stacked.
levels.2-8.hint1: Variance is the mean of the squared distance from the mean. Epsilon avoids division by zero on constant rows; this component has no extra trainable scale or bias.
ui.tensorProbeHelp: Tensor inputs are read-only. Switch cases to see other data. Hover a node for its full values.
levels.1-8.title: Partial derivatives
levels.1-8.description: Inputs: a and b. For f(a,b) = a·b + exp(a), build ∂f/∂a. Let only a vary and treat b as a constant. This is a partial derivative.
levels.1-8.hint1: When differentiating with respect to a, what is the slope of a·b? b does not change with a.
levels.1-8.hint2: The derivative of a·b with respect to a is b; exp(a) is its own derivative. Add the two.
levels.1-9.title: Another direction
levels.1-9.description: Inputs: a and b. For f(a,b) = a·exp(a·b), build ∂f/∂b, treating a as a constant. The same f has a different partial derivative for each variable. Stack them all and you get the gradient: the direction in which f rises fastest. Chapter 3 uses it to walk downhill.
levels.1-9.hint1: The outer a stays constant. Differentiating exp(a·b) with respect to b also needs the derivative of a·b.
levels.1-9.hint2: One a outside, another from the chain rule: a·a·exp(a·b).
levels.1-10.title: Backpropagation by hand
levels.1-10.description: Inputs: w, x and b. One neuron: z = w·x + b, output f = sigmoid(z). Build ∂f/∂w. Walk back from the output and multiply by each step's derivative as you go. That is backpropagation. After this, the engine does it for you: autodiff and the expression box unlock.
levels.1-10.hint1: Let z = w·x + b. The derivative of f with respect to z is σ′(z), the part you built in 1-5; multiply it by the derivative of z with respect to w.
levels.1-10.hint2: The answer is σ′(w·x + b)·x. Remember the final x.

gradView.title: Gradient graph
gradView.intro: On top is your circuit; values flow left to right. Below is the mirror the engine draws from it: gradients start at the output and flow right to left, multiplied at each part by that part's own derivative (written on the wire). A value used several times receives several gradients, added at a "+". That is automatic differentiation, the same thing you built by hand in 1-10.
gradView.parameters.initial: On training levels the gradient is taken with respect to the parameters θ (what training changes), not the data. These are the parameters before training; open it again after training to see gradients at the current parameters.
gradView.parameters.current: On training levels the gradient is taken with respect to the parameters θ (what training changes), not the data. These are the parameters you just trained.
gradView.trainingData: Values come from one batch of this level's training data.
gradView.attachedLoss: On this level the engine computes the loss after your output: it compares the probabilities with the right answers using cross entropy. That part is drawn too (labelled "cross entropy"), so the gradient starts at loss. It is only drawn for you to see; your circuit is unchanged.
gradView.openHint: See how the engine derives gradients from this graph
gradView.revealButton: See how the engine does it
gradView.revealIntro: This is the neuron you just did, f = σ(w·x + b). On top, the forward pass. Below, the backward pass the engine generates: start at f and multiply by each local derivative on the way back. It is exactly your σ′(w·x + b)·x; from now on the engine does it for you.
levels.3-1.title: One step downhill
levels.3-1.description: From this chapter on, circuits learn by themselves. The smallest model: multiply a parameter w by the input x to get a prediction w·x, which should equal the target t. First we need a score for "how far off": square the difference w·x − t, giving L = (w·x − t)². It is never negative, 0 on a hit and larger the further off it is. A "smaller is better" number like this is called a loss function, and training means pushing it down. How? The gradient ∂L/∂w points where L rises fastest, so take a small step the other way. Input w, x, t; output w after one step: w − 0.1·∂L/∂w.
levels.3-1.hint1: Chain rule for ∂L/∂w: a square on the outside, w·x − t inside.
levels.3-1.hint2: ∂L/∂w = 2(w·x − t)·x. Multiply by 0.1 and subtract it from w.
levels.3-2.title: The gradient is a list
levels.3-2.description: Now w and x are vectors of length 3; t is still a single number. The prediction is the dot product w·x = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃, and the loss is still L = (w·x − t)². Change only w₁ and hold the rest still: how fast L moves is the partial derivative ∂L/∂w₁. It is the chain rule from the last level: a square outside, and w·x − t differentiated by w₁ gives x₁. Do the same for w₂ and w₃ and line them up, [∂L/∂w₁, ∂L/∂w₂, ∂L/∂w₃]: that list is the gradient ∂L/∂w. Inputs w [3], x [3], t (one number). Output the gradient [3]. The judge also tries length 5, so you cannot write each component out by hand.
levels.3-2.hint1: Write ∂L/∂w₁ first: it differs from the last level's ∂L/∂w only by a subscript. Then look at ∂L/∂w₂ and ∂L/∂w₃. Which part is the same in all three?
levels.3-2.hint2: 2(w·x − t) is one number; multiply it by the whole of x. Broadcasting spreads it out.
levels.3-3.title: Mean squared error
levels.3-3.description: The last two levels had one sample, so the loss was a single squared difference (p − t)². Real training looks at a batch: p is 8 predictions, t is 8 targets, so there are 8 differences. Square each, then average, and you are back to one number: the mean squared error (MSE), the batch version of 3-1's loss. With a single sample the two are identical. Output shape [1]. Pass it and it becomes your part.
levels.3-3.hint1: p − t times itself is the square.
levels.3-3.hint2: After squaring, use the mean you built.
levels.3-4.title: Let it run
levels.3-4.description:
The plot at the bottom right shows 16 points, roughly on a line. Goal: find a straight line that fits them.

· Input x: the points' horizontal coordinates.
· Input t: their vertical coordinates, the answers.

You build:
1. The prediction p = w·x + b. Take w and b from the "Parameter" part on the left; they start at 0 and the engine adjusts them during training. w and b are single numbers; broadcasting spreads them over all 16 positions, so all 16 predictions come out at once. Samples computed together like this are called a batch.
2. Feed p and t into your MSE and wire the result to the output loss: how far the predictions still are from the answers.

Then press start: the engine repeats "forward → backward → update" 60 times (the training loop on the right). Your only choice is the learning rate, how far each step goes. Get loss below 0.05 within 60 steps.
Grading uses these same training samples, not a separate test set.
levels.3-4.hint1: Place two "Parameter" nodes for w and b: multiply x by w, add b, and that is the prediction p. Feed p and t into MSE, and MSE into the output loss. There is only one neuron here, so zero weights cannot trap several hidden units into doing the same thing.
levels.3-4.hint2: The default rate is too small to get there in 60 steps; too large and each step overshoots the valley and bounces further out. Try between 0.1 and 0.5.
levels.train_diverged: Getting further away: the learning rate is too large, and every step overshoots the valley. Lower it.
levels.train_slow: All 60 steps used and loss is still {loss}. Steps too small? Try a larger learning rate.
ui.stepHelp: Take one step: watch values flow forward, gradients flow back and the parameters move.
ui.gradHelp: Gradient of the loss with respect to this value, ∂loss/∂(·)
ui.stepPhase.forward: ① Forward: data flows through the network, loss = {loss}
ui.stepPhase.backward: ② Backward: the gradient flows back from loss; each node gets ∂loss/∂(·)
ui.stepPhase.update: ③ Update: every parameter θ ← θ − η·∂loss/∂θ
levels.3-5.title: Cross entropy
levels.3-5.description: A classification model outputs a row of class probabilities p; label t gives the answer, not a class number. If the second of three classes is correct, t = [0,1,0]: 1 for the correct class and 0 elsewhere, called one-hot encoding. Multiplying and summing selects the log probability of the correct class. Compute −Σ t·log p per row, then average the rows: cross entropy. Inputs [4×3], output [1]; tests also change row and class counts. Pass to keep the component.
levels.3-5.hint1: Take the logarithm of p, multiply by t and sum the last axis; use Mean across rows, then negate. Softmax turns arbitrary class scores into probabilities summing to 1, exactly what p needs here.
levels.3-5.hint2: Why −log(probability of the correct class)? Multiplying independent samples’ correct-answer probabilities gives the likelihood. Maximizing that product is equivalent to maximizing the sum of logs, or minimizing the mean negative log: negative log likelihood. Unlike squared error on probabilities, Softmax with cross entropy retains a large score gradient when confidently wrong, usually making correction easier—not guaranteeing faster learning every time.
levels.neuron.title: One neuron
levels.neuron.description:
Look at a single point x = (x₁, x₂) first. Give it a score: multiply each coordinate by its own weight, add them up, then add a bias b:
y = x₁w₁ + x₂w₂ + b = x·w + b
A dot product plus a bias — that is one neuron. w and b are its parameters; they are what training adjusts.

The tests also stack 5 points into a [5×2] input (one point per row). Without changing a single part, your circuit outputs 5 scores. Feeding one computation a whole stack of data at once is called a batch.
levels.neuron.hint1: Chapter 2’s dot product sums along the last axis; then add b with an adder.
levels.neuron.hint2: For x [5×2], the dot product sums along the last axis (each point’s two coordinates), giving one number per row; b broadcasts across those 5 numbers. Don’t sum along the first axis (the point index).
levels.layer.title: A layer
levels.layer.description:
Several neurons scoring every point at once make a layer. Stand each neuron’s w on end as one column of a matrix W; put their biases in a vector b.

You could build last level’s circuit 3 times, but the matrix product xW takes a dot product of every point (a row of x) with every neuron (a column of W) in one go; adding b broadcasts each neuron’s bias down the rows.
y = xW + b has shape [points × neurons]: row i, column j is neuron j’s score for point i.
Passing unlocks the Linear layer part.
levels.layer.hint1: x [points×coords] times W [coords×neurons] gives [points×neurons]. A column of W is one neuron’s weights, not a row.
levels.layer.hint2: Add b [neurons] to xW: broadcasting gives every point the same biases.
levels.3-6.title: Draw a boundary
levels.3-6.description:
40 points, two classes. Start with one point (x₁, x₂): its score for class 1 is x₁w₁₁ + x₂w₂₁ + b₁, a dot product plus a bias: one "neuron". Two classes need two neurons; stand each one's weights up as a column and you have W [2×2], with their biases in b [2]. Now stack the 40 points one per row into x [40×2]. Matrix multiplication xW takes the dot product of every row with every column (2-6), so all 40 points × 2 neurons are scored at once, giving [40×2]; then add b, broadcast to each row. A set of neurons side by side, applied to a whole batch, is a layer. Finish with softmax for class probabilities; the engine computes cross entropy against the labels. Adjust the learning rate to reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy within 80 steps.
Grading uses these same training samples, not a separate test set.
levels.3-6.hint1: Use trainable parameters for W [2×2] and b [2]. Matrix-multiply xW, add b, then apply softmax. Nothing depends on how many rows x has, so the same circuit works for 1 point or 40.
levels.3-6.hint2: The default learning rate is deliberately small. Increase it and watch both loss and accuracy; output probabilities, not the loss.
levels.3-7.title: Remember the last step
levels.3-7.description: Plain SGD uses only the current gradient. Momentum accumulates past gradients into a velocity m, moving faster in a consistent direction: m′ = 0.9m + g, then w′ = w − 0.1m′. Given scalar w, gradient g and previous momentum m, output the updated w. This lesson builds one momentum step, not Adam.
levels.3-7.hint1: Multiply the previous momentum m by 0.9, then add the new gradient g.
levels.3-7.hint2: Multiply that new momentum by 0.1 and subtract it from w. The output is the updated parameter, not the momentum.
levels.3-8.title: Different scales, different steps
levels.3-8.description:
Two features: one tiny but useful, one huge and only noise. A single learning rate is too slow for one and too wild for the other, so no SGD setting works. Switch the optimizer to Adam in the right panel: it sizes each parameter's steps separately. Reach loss below 0.15 and 100% accuracy within 600 steps.
Grading uses these same training samples, not a separate test set.
levels.3-8.hint1: Keep the model y = softmax(xW + b), with W [2×2] and b [2]. The challenge is the update rule, not a bigger network.
levels.3-8.hint2: If one learning rate is too slow for one direction and too large for the other, try Adam. Reset parameters for a fair comparison.
levels.3-9.title: Bend the boundary
levels.3-9.description:
64 points in two concentric rings; no straight line separates them. Add another layer: the first, x·W₁ + b₁, has more than 2 neurons, one per column of W₁ (say [2×8], so 8), turning each point into 8 new features; pass them through an activation, then a second layer ·W₂ + b₂ ([8×2]) scores the two classes → softmax. The middle layer is called a hidden layer, and it lets the network bend the plane itself. Loss below 0.15 and at least 95% accuracy within 300 steps.
Two purely linear layers xW₁W₂ still equal x(W₁W₂); adding biases still leaves a single affine calculation. Without an activation between layers, stacking more cannot bend the boundary.
Grading uses these same training samples, not a separate test set.
levels.3-9.hint1: Try h = ReLU(xW₁ + b₁), then y = softmax(hW₂ + b₂). Hidden units can combine several straight boundaries into a curved region.
levels.3-9.hint2: Initialize weights randomly. If hidden units have identical incoming and outgoing weights, they produce the same values, receive the same gradients and updates, and keep acting like one unit. Random initialization gives weights small differences at the start, not random changes every step; biases may start at zero. The single neuron in 3-4 had no duplicate hidden units. Output [64×2] probabilities; if training stalls, adjust the learning rate or compare optimizers.
levels.train_accuracy: The step budget is exhausted. Loss is low enough, but accuracy is only {accuracy}, below the target.
levels.4-1.title: Characters to numbers
levels.4-1.description: Computers work with numbers. Give each character an ID, then turn it into a row with just one 1. Input k lists class IDs 0 through V−1; its length sets the number of classes.
levels.4-1.hint1: Unsqueeze idx on the last axis to compare every ID with every entry of k.
levels.4-1.hint2: Multiply ge(idx, k) by ge(k, idx). Both comparisons are true only for equal IDs.
levels.4-2.title: Look up a row
levels.4-2.description:
A one-hot times table picks out the matching row: every character gets its own list of numbers (a vector).
This level tries tables of different sizes, so the row numbers can’t be hard-coded; compute them from the table. New part, Range: input n, output [0, 1, …, n−1].
Passing unlocks the Embedding part: the same result without the multiplication.
levels.4-2.hint1: Feed table into Dimension size (axis 0) to get its row count, then into Range to get every row number.
levels.4-2.hint2: Row numbers go into One-hot’s k port and idx into its idx port; matrix-multiply the one-hot matrix by table.
levels.4-3.title: The next character
levels.4-3.description:
See one character, guess the next. The corpus begins with little: its adjacent training pairs are l→i, i→t, t→t, t→l and l→e. A character ID is its index in the vocabulary of distinct characters; the vocabulary size is V. Inputs l i t t l pair with answers i t t l e: position i targets character i+1. x holds the current character IDs; the answers are the following characters, and y outputs their probabilities [N×V]. Build a V×V parameter table: one row per character, scoring every character that might follow it. After training, "Write" in the right panel lets it keep going on its own.
Training and grading use all adjacent character pairs in this corpus. Cross entropy must fall below approximately 2.181574 (a corpus-derived threshold); no unseen text is tested.
levels.4-3.hint1: Gather rows from the parameter table using x as the indices.
levels.4-3.hint2: Apply softmax to the gathered logits and output y. Adam minimizes cross entropy; adjust the learning rate if needed.
levels.4-4.title: Draw a character
levels.4-4.description: The model gives probabilities. Arrange them along a line and throw a random number between 0 and 1 to choose a segment.
levels.4-4.hint1: Multiply p by the supplied upper triangular matrix to get cumulative probabilities.
levels.4-4.hint2: Compare u with each cumulative probability using ge, then sum the comparisons to get a scalar class ID.
levels.reshape.title: Reshape
levels.reshape.description: Turn x from [N,2,D] into [N,2D]: join each sample's two vectors into one row. Tensor values are stored as one ordered sequence: traverse the last axis first, then the preceding one. Reshape only rereads this sequence with different row breaks, preserving both order and element count. Thus [2,2,3] can become [2,6] or [12], but not [5,2]. Transpose instead swaps axes, changing the reading order. N and D vary between tests, so derive dimensions from x rather than hard-coding them.
levels.reshape.hint1: Reshape’s shape attribute may contain one −1, meaning “work out this length yourself”. That is a different thing from axis −1 meaning the last axis.
levels.reshape.hint2: Feed x into Dimension size (axis 0) to get N and wire it into Reshape’s Target dimension 0 port; set the shape attribute to [1, −1]: the wire replaces dimension 0 with N and −1 works out 2D.
levels.4-5.title: One more character
levels.4-5.description: One character is short-sighted: after h may come e or a. Each row of x holds two previous characters [N×2]: look up their vectors, join them, pass through a hidden layer and output next-character probabilities. Training and grading use the same fixed 512 two-character contexts. Cross entropy must fall below approximately 1.639788 (a corpus-derived threshold). This does not test unseen text.
levels.4-5.hint1: Gather from E with x shaped [N,2] to get [N,2,D], then reshape to [N,2D], just as in the previous reshape lesson.
levels.4-5.hint2: Add a nonlinear hidden layer, use a linear layer for V candidate-character scores, then Softmax. The threshold is below the best cross entropy using only the last character on this batch; grading checks loss, not how you wire the two characters.
worker.generation_unavailable: This lesson does not support text generation.
worker.invalid_probabilities: The graph must output finite, nonnegative character probabilities with a positive total.
ui.generateHelp: Uses the parameters from your latest training; untrained, it writes gibberish. Each step takes the context at the end of the existing text, runs a forward pass, samples one character from the last position's probabilities, appends it, and repeats. Generation does not update parameters. Low temperature plays safe, high takes chances.

levels.5-1.title: Who should look at whom?
levels.5-1.description: Each position compares q (what am I looking for?) with each k (what is here?). A larger q·k means greater relevance. T positions give a T×T score table. Wider vectors usually give larger dot products, making Softmax too sharp and nearly selecting only one position; divide by √D, obtaining width D from the input shape.
levels.5-1.hint1: Transpose the last two axes of k, then multiply q by kᵀ. Here q and k are supplied. In 5-5, both come from the same character-plus-position vectors multiplied by two different trainable matrices. Their meanings are not assigned by hand.
levels.5-1.hint2: Use Size for D, the length of q’s last axis, take its square root, then divide the dot products by it.
levels.5-2.title: Do not peek ahead
levels.5-2.description: Input position i predicts character i+1. It may read its own input character at i (the diagonal) and earlier positions, but not later ones: no peeking at the answer. Keep scores on and below the diagonal and replace every entry above it with exactly -1e9, giving zero probability after softmax. Tests compare scores themselves. T varies, so derive the mask size from the input shape.
levels.5-2.hint1: Build row and column indices with arange and unsqueeze. ge(row, column) is 1 for positions that may be read.
levels.5-2.hint2: Compute scores × mask + (1 − mask) × -1e9. Do not use -Infinity or another negative constant: the masked scores must numerically match -1e9.
levels.5-3.title: Mix the useful information
levels.5-3.description: Connect the previous two levels: mask future positions, apply Softmax per row for weights summing to 1, then take a weighted average of the rows of v. k determines relevance; v is the content being carried, and their widths may differ. Each position mixes its own and earlier content; q and k determine where to look and how much.
levels.5-3.hint1: Scaled attention scores → Causal mask → Softmax along the last axis, then Matrix multiply by v.
levels.5-3.hint2: Multiply the attention probabilities by v. Future positions must receive zero weight; each row may still attend to itself.
levels.5-4.title: Give each character a position
levels.5-4.description: Attention sees content, not order. Build embed_pos with inputs idx, tokens and positions: look up each character ID, then add the vector for position 0, 1, 2… The same character can now have different vectors at different positions.
levels.5-4.hint1: Gather from tokens using idx. Use the last axis of idx to find the sequence length and arange to generate position IDs.
levels.5-4.hint2: Gather those position IDs from positions and add the result to the token embeddings; broadcast the position vectors across any batch axis.
levels.5-5.title: Learn with attention
levels.5-5.description:
Assemble the pieces: character vectors plus position vectors, one matrix each for q, k and v, attention, then one more matrix to score every character, and softmax. Each training window contains T+1 characters: the first T are inputs and the last T are answers shifted one position ahead (here T=8). Position i predicts character i+1 using only inputs at or before i. Output [batch,position,V] gives each of the T positions its own probability distribution for the next character. Since the input text is already given, training practices all T questions in parallel in one forward pass; this is not generating T new characters at once. Generation samples one next character, appends it to the context, then runs the model again. Let it write once trained. One attention head cannot form real sentences yet; the next chapter stacks it into a real Transformer.
Training and grading use the same 128 fixed windows. Cross entropy averaged over all positions must be below 1.75; this is not an independent unseen-text test.
levels.5-5.hint1: Start with Token + position embedding. Multiply the same vectors by three different trainable matrices for q, k and v, then use Attention. They start with no fixed meanings; the same prediction loss trains all three matrices to make matching and carrying content useful.
levels.5-5.hint2: Project the attention output to vocabulary logits and apply softmax over the vocabulary. Keep the causal mask so a prediction cannot read future characters.
levels.6-1.title: Look in several ways at once
levels.6-1.description:
Build multi_head with inputs q, k and v: split their channels into two heads, apply causal attention independently in each head, then join the outputs. For D=4, each token's channels [a,b,c,d] split into head 0 [a,b] and head 1 [c,d]. Reshape [B,T,4] to [B,T,2,2], then transpose to [B,2,T,2]; each head attends across T positions, not across heads. Transpose back before reshaping the outputs to [B,T,4]. Derive sequence lengths and channel widths from the inputs rather than fixing the test shape. Tensors in this chapter carry a leading batch dimension B to process several passages at once, with input shape [B,T,D].
Channels are vector components at each position; a head is a group computing its own attention weights. What it attends to is learned, not assigned by hand.
levels.6-1.hint1: Reshape q, k and v to expose two heads, then transpose so attention sees the sequence and per-head channels as its last two axes. Preserve the leading batch axis B: reshape to [B,T,2,D/2], then swap the middle axes to get [B,2,T,D/2].
levels.6-1.hint2: Apply attention in each head, transpose back and reshape to merge the head channels. Scale each head’s scores by the square root of its key channel width; projections belong outside multi_head.
levels.6-2.title: Think at each position
levels.6-2.description: Build Feed-forward network from x, w1, b1, w2 and b2: widen vectors with w1 and b1, apply ReLU, then return to the original width with w2 and b2. This is chapter 3’s two-layer nonlinear network: attention exchanges information between positions; this processes each position individually with shared weights.
levels.6-2.hint1: Compute ReLU(x @ w1 + b1). Broadcast the bias across sequence and batch axes.
levels.6-2.hint2: Multiply the hidden activations by w2, then add b2. The output must return to the input channel width; do not normalize or mix positions.
levels.6-3.title: Build a Transformer block
levels.6-3.description: A Transformer block combines attention (exchange information between positions) and a feed-forward network (process each position), each with layer normalization and a residual connection. A residual adds the branch result to its original input; pre-normalization means normalizing before branch computation. Supply x and eight weights/biases: wq, wk, wv, wo, w1, b1, w2, b2.
levels.6-3.hint1: Let n = Layer normalization(x). Use Matrix multiply for q = n·wq, k = n·wk and v = n·wv; multiply Multi-head attention’s result by wo, then add the original x to get h. A residual x + f(x) lets the branch learn a correction; f(x)=0 preserves x. The addition’s direct derivative with respect to x is 1, giving gradients a direct route to earlier layers, using chapter 1’s differentiation rules.
levels.6-3.hint2: Then y = h + Feed-forward network(Layer normalization(h), w1, b1, w2, b2). Along the channel axis—the vector at each position—subtract the mean and divide by √(variance + ε), centering at 0 with variance near 1 except for constant vectors. Controlling branch-input scale helps prevent growth or shrinkage across layers and stabilizes training; it does not bound every intermediate value.
levels.6-4.title: Let your Transformer write
levels.6-4.description:
Build a small GPT: token and position embeddings, two Transformer blocks, a final layer normalization, a vocabulary projection and softmax. Train it to predict the next character, then generate text: take the context at the end of the existing text, run a forward pass, sample one character from the last position's probabilities, append it, and repeat. This continuation loop uses the trained weights without updating any parameters; only training updates them. Each block needs its own trainable weights; causal attention prevents peeking ahead. Training takes about 1 minute on CPU; WebGPU makes it much faster.
Each update trains on 8 sampled windows. Every 250 steps and at the end, evaluate without updates on 400 fixed windows from the same corpus. Passing requires their mean cross entropy below 1.1—not the last minibatch’s loss, and not an independent test set. Low loss does not guarantee fluent generation or good predictions on new text.
levels.6-4.hint1: Start with embed_pos. Give each block its own query, key, value and output projection matrices, plus feed-forward weights w1, b1, w2 and b2. Match channel dimensions between components.
levels.6-4.hint2: After the second block, apply layernorm, project to vocabulary logits and softmax over characters. Train with Adam; generation uses your latest trained parameters.
loop.title: The training loop: five things, every step
loop.data.name: Take a batch
loop.data.fixed: The same samples every step, computed together (3-4)
loop.data.resample: A fresh random batch from the corpus every step
loop.forward.name: Forward
loop.forward.note: Compute predictions with current parameters. The level supplies data and answers; you choose wiring and parameter shapes. Training changes parameter values, not wiring or answers.
loop.loss.name: Loss
loop.loss.note: Compare predictions with answers for this step’s training batch to get a smaller-is-better number (3-3 MSE, 3-5 cross entropy). The level explains which data are graded and the loss threshold; classification levels also require accuracy.
loop.backward.name: Backward
loop.backward.note: The chain rule gives every parameter its gradient; you did it by hand in 3-1 and 3-2, now the engine does it
loop.update.name: Update
loop.update.sgd: Each parameter takes a small step against its gradient: w ← w − {lr}·gradient (3-1)
loop.update.adam: Adam: each parameter sizes its own step from its history, base step {lr} (3-9, 3-10)
loop.repeat: Return to step 1, {steps} times in all. Lower loss means better predictions on the measured data, not necessarily on new data. Memorizing training data without handling new data is called overfitting.
coach.title: Getting started
coach.mul: This level asks for −x. The idea: multiply x by −1. First drag "Multiply" from the parts on the left onto the canvas (a click works too).
coach.wireX: Inputs are on a part's left, outputs on its right. Press on the square to the right of x, drag it to the a port on the left of Multiply, and let go.
coach.const: Now add a "Constant" and wire it to Multiply's b port. Select it and set its value to −1 under Properties on the right.
coach.wireY: Finally wire Multiply's output to y. The live values on the right then show y; compare it with "Expected" below it.
coach.run: If they match, press "Run tests" on the right: the engine checks your circuit on many values of x. Pass them all and the part is yours.
